canonicalExplanation.summary: `<video>` and `<audio>` with the `controls` attribute give everyone play, pause, volume and seeking — including by keyboard. But controls don't make **speech** accessible: add **captions** with `<track kind="captions">` (a WebVTT file) and link a **transcript**. Third-party embeds (`<iframe>` from video sites) load another company's code and cookies — give them a `title`, and prefer privacy-friendly embed options.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Your lesson video is great — unless you're deaf, in a noisy train, or can't play sound at work. Then it's silent moving pictures. And the embedded player may start tracking visitors before they even press play. A lesson video includes native controls, synchronized captions, and a linked transcript. In this lesson you'll embed accessible time-based media and explain cross-origin or third-party privacy concerns.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Relative and absolute URLs**, **Paragraph and inline meaning**, **Images and alternative text**, and **External navigation safety** (third-party content).

sections.heading: Third-party embeds and privacy

includes: Embed video/audio with controls, captions via track, and a transcript.
Explain privacy concerns of third-party embeds and mitigate them.
excludes: Streaming formats like HLS and DASH.

outcomes: Embed accessible time-based media and explain cross-origin or third-party privacy concerns.

examples.title: An accessible lesson video
examples.situation: A lesson video includes native controls, synchronized captions, and a linked transcript.
walkthrough: **Native controls:** `<video controls>` gives keyboard-operable play, pause and seeking.
**Synchronized captions:** `<track kind="captions" src="intro.en.vtt" default>` shows the speech in time with the video.
**Linked transcript:** the figcaption links to a full transcript page learners can read and search.
examples.result: Learners who can't hear, or can't play sound, can still follow the whole lesson video.

examples.title: The embed that tracked everyone
examples.situation: A course homepage embeds three videos with standard iframes. Privacy tools show third-party cookies set on every visit.
walkthrough: Each iframe loads the platform's scripts immediately.
Visitors are tracked even if they never play a video.
Fix: use the platform's privacy-enhanced domain or a click-to-load thumbnail, add `title="Intro to HTML video"`, and mention it in the privacy notice.
examples.result: Videos load only when a visitor chooses to play, and each iframe has an accessible name.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Adding controls makes spoken video content accessible without captions or a transcript.
misconceptions.correction: Controls make the player operable, but spoken content is only accessible to deaf and hard-of-hearing users through synchronized captions and a transcript. Both are needed alongside native controls.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "An accessible lesson video", which two additions serve people who can't hear?

analogy.example: A video without captions is like a **TV show in a noisy airport**: you see the screen but miss everything said. Captions are the text on screen; a transcript is the printed script you can read later.
usefulFor: seeing captions and transcript as different tools
limitations: TV captions are often burned in; web captions can be switched on and off.
An embed is like a TV that also watches who's in the room.

remediation.explanation: Checklist for media: **controls? captions track? transcript link? no autoplay with sound? third-party embed titled and privacy-safe?**

recap.summary: To embed accessible time-based media, use native controls, synchronized captions with track, and a linked transcript, and avoid autoplay with sound. Third-party embeds load another origin's code and cookies — title them and use privacy-friendly loading.
